text.p: European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn on Thursday called on the public to recognise the extent of the health problems posed by smoking and said Europe should be bold enough to outlaw tobacco advertising.
Flynn praised the U.S. administration's recent move to impose tougher restrictions on the sale and advertising of tobacco and said that Europe should follow suit.

"The recent announcement by President Clinton shows the political will to act against a powerful interest group, and I applaud that," Flynn told a European anti-smoking conference here, according to his prepared speech.
"We need the same courage here in Europe to finally outlaw advertising of tobacco and stop the addiction of generations," Flynn said.
"I am strongly convinced that tobacco control is a global issue," he said.
In August, President Bill Clinton endorsed a plan to impose tight new controls on tobacco sales and advertising.

Flynn said smoking kills up to half a million people in the European Union annually, and that the public perception of the danger was lagging behind awareness of other health problems such as drug abuse.
He blamed the social acceptability of smoking and ignorance of its harms on positive portrayals of smoking in the media, especially in advertising and product sponsorship.
Flynn said European programmes to curb smoking and prevent cancer had been no match for tobacco makers' efforts "to hook new smokers."
"They have cynically used sport, film stars, pop stars, fashion models, the lot, to sell their addiction to our children," the commissioner said.

Singling out sponsorship of televised sporting events by tobacco companies as a problem area, Flynn said the EU was looking into the issue in connection with its "Television Without Frontiers" directive.
"It may be that the existing definition of 'advertising' is too loose and allows tobacco firms to get away with their scandalous behaviour," Flynn said.

Noting that television advertising of tobacco is already banned in Europe, Flynn said a Commission proposal to ban tobacco ads in places other than inside retailers' premises, COM(92)196, had failed to win the support of a majority of EU member states.

He said the proposed directive would cover tobacco advertising on outdoor posters, in newspapers and magazines and would also cover "indirect advertising, such as sponsorship and use of the brand name for other products."

Europe was also continuing to address the issues of smoking in public places and at the workplace, and he said it was time to effectively apply the principle that "the right to health of non-smokers prevails over the right of smokers to smoke".

Flynn referred to a campaign by tobacco giant Philip Morris in the European press a few months ago asserting that drinking water, eating biscuits and using pepper were more dangerous than passive smoking.
He called it a "deceitful campaign" and added: "How cynical and untruthful can you get!"
The commissioner brushed aside the notion that the EU's efforts to curb smoking and prevent cancer should start with reducing EU support for the tobacco industry.

"In my view, the main strategy in reducing smoking in the European Union should not focus on tobacco subsidies but on what can be done to prevent people from starting the habit, and helping those already hooked," he said.
The EU accounted for only 5.4 percent of world tobacco production -- an amount which could easily be replaced by production from elsewhere if subsidies were withdrawn, he said.
